title: UK long-term borrowing costs highest since 1998 ahead of October Budget
description: Long-term government borrowing costs have risen to a 28-year high, putting further pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham ahead of his first Budget n
body: Long-term government borrowing costs have risen to a 28-year high, putting further pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham ahead of his first Budget next month.The yield on a 30-year gilt — a loan to the British government — rose to 5.89% on Tuesday, the highest since 1998.Borrowing costs in the US, Japan and Europe have hit similar highs in recent days, reflecting investors' concerns about inflation, state borrowing levels and spending levels by large tech companies on AI.Burnham told the House of Commons his government's "bedrock", as it seeks to tackle the cost-of-living crisis, will be "fiscal responsibility".All of those factors will make the Budget process trickier for Burnham, who on Tuesday addressed MPs for the first time as prime minister, and his Chancellor John Healey. Burnham told the House of Commons the economy and the cost of living were "the biggest issues facing the country".Higher borrowing costs will reduce the amount of headroom the government has against its self-imposed fiscal rules, limiting the amount Healey can spend on consumer-friendly measures to ease the cost of living. Despite the squeezed public finances, Burnham said said he would bring about "more substantial change" to ease living costs."Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be," he added.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of "living in the past"."His diagnosis is completely wrong," she told the House of Commons. "His theory of growth is completely wrong. He thinks that if Government spends more money, we will all get richer. "That is not how this works."The chancellor has previously said he will stick to a set of fiscal rules imposed by his predecessor Rachel Reeves that restrict borrowing. These rules are designed to help markets have clarity about the path of borrowing.The more that is forecast to be spent on interest payments, the more likely that there will be a squeeze on spending or some form of tax rise to meet these rules.On top of that, higher government rates can feed through to higher business and household borrowing costs, and so weigh on the economy.Burnham was already facing a tough balancing act with taxing and spending, due to pressures on defence and the cost of living.As well as the rise to 30-year gilt yields, the yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt rose to 5.22% on Tuesday. This is its highest rate since June 2008, at the height of the global financial crisis. Gilt yields move counter to the value of the bonds, meaning their prices fall when yields rise.Around the world there are warning lights flashing from the markets for government debt.Global markets reacted in particular after suggestions in the US that its central bank could raise rates. Japan is also facing pressure to raise rates.The Chancellor is in the USA attending a meeting of global finance ministers and central bankers. He told the G20 that the UK had the fastest growth in the G7 in 2026 so far, that productivity was improving and that the UK was cutting its borrowing at the fastest rate of the major economies.US borrowing costs hit a fresh high on Tuesday as renewed strikes in the Middle East pushed up oil prices and heightened concerns over inflation.Karen Ward, JP Morgan's chief market strategist for Europe, said governments around the world want to increase spending and are turning to borrowing to fund it.And she told the BBC's World at One they are increasingly having to compete with major technology companies raising money to invest in the AI revolution, pushing up the amount of interest being charged."Markets are getting a lot more choice about who they are going to lend to and at what interest rates," she added.Burnham has rolled out a series of interventions to support consumers and businesses since entering Downing Street, and is expected to prioritise further measures to ease the cost of living in the Budget on 28 October. Ward urged Burnham and Healey to set out how they will fund any fresh spending on defence and the cost of living, and how those lending the government money will be paid back.Kathleen Brooks, research director at investment company XTB, told the BBC News Channel: "Of course, this is red lights flashing.""We are used to pockets of volatility, it has been volatile few months," she says.But record levels of government debt and a record tax take mean "these are not comfortable times for the new government and the new chancellor," she says.Every time bond yields rise, the UK has to pay more on the debt interest, she says.

schema.headline: UK long-term borrowing costs highest since 1998 ahead of October Budget

title: Spaces in male prisons in England and Wales fall to lowest level of year, sources say
description: An investment of £110m, which will come from existing budgets, will be used to convert unused office space, laundry rooms and storage space into cells
body: An investment of £110m, which will come from existing budgets, will be used to convert unused office space, laundry rooms and storage space into cells, the MoJ said.The justice secretary told the BBC prisoners being released early did not mean "freedom" and victims would have a say in restrictions placed on those criminals.Asked where clothes would be washed if laundry rooms were converted into cells, Norris told BBC Breakfast: "Of course we're going to make sure that the prisons can still function properly."This is a creative look, as I say, around our estate and being able to use some space that we can re-prioritise."Norris said he suspected the number of extra prison spaces created from freeing up existing space within prisons would be "landing somewhere in the middle" of 200 and 900.But the chairman of the Prison Officers' Association, Mark Fairhurst, said: "You can create as much additional space as you like, and build as many new prisons as you like, but where are the staff coming from to supervise people? Nobody wants to be a prison officer anymore."Prisons in England and Wales are running at 97% capacity.Under the early release scheme some 4,500 prisoners are now expected to start being let out of prison in tranches from October.On Sunday, the prime minister told BBC Breakfast anyone convicted of manslaughter would be excluded from the scheme, following a campaign from PC Andrew Harper's family to block the release of two men convicted over his killing in 2019.Extra prison space would also be created by deporting more foreign prisoners and releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences.Government figures show there were 10,134 foreign nationals held in custody on 30 June, 3,283 of whom were on remand and would not be eligible for deportation.In the year to June, 5,962 foreign offenders were sent back to their home countries - the highest rate of deportations since 2017 and a 12% increase on the previous year.

schema.headline: Spaces in male prisons in England and Wales fall to lowest level of year, sources say

title: Sexual assaults in Ceuta happening almost every day, prosecutors say
description: Spanish prosecutors say 23 sexual assaults, including nine against children, have been recorded in Ceuta since the mass influx of migrants into the Sp
body: Spanish prosecutors say 23 sexual assaults, including nine against children, have been recorded in Ceuta since the mass influx of migrants into the Spanish exclave  at the end of July.That number meant there was almost one case every day, Ceuta's chief prosecutor Silvia Rojas said.She told El País newspaper migrant girls were "particularly vulnerable because of their irregular status in the territory".At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July and although most have returned, as many as 5,000 remain - leading to unrest in the autonomous city in North Africa and a crisis for Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.Between 1,400 and 1,600 of the estimated 5,000 migrants still in Ceuta are children, according to Rojas.Among the suspected attackers are four Moroccans, three Spaniards and a Belgian, Efe news agency reports.There have been scenes of violence in recent days as tensions flare up between migrants and local residents. Sánchez called the second meeting of his national security council in a week on Tuesday to tackle the issue.Rojas said the influx had led to an exponential increase in sexual assault, and many victims did not file a report, either out of fear of because of their "current situation in Ceuta". The Spanish Society of Epidemiology said the border crisis had highlighted the difficulty in detecting and tackling violence against migrant women and girls.One 24-year-old woman from Morocco told the BBC she had "put her life in danger" by travelling to Ceuta, and described being sexually assaulted while sleeping among a group of men and women. "I was shocked… If I had known this, I wouldn't have come."Emergency doctor Susana Ascaso said last month her department at Ceuta University Hospital had treated several sexual assault victims, including one who was just 10 years old.Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said a multi-million euro aid package had been approved by the cabinet that would help provide essential services and cover care for unaccompanied children.The territory's conservative mayor, Juan Jesús Vivas, has called on Spaniards to take part in demonstrations across mainland Spain in support of Ceuta on Wednesday, which coincides with the city's annual holiday.The Spanish government is facing bitter criticism from its opponents for its handling of the crisis. The hard-right Vox party said Sánchez had not "lost control of Ceuta - he has handed it over".Arantxa Campos, president of the Ceuta Employers' Confederation, told the BBC: "We can't do anything unless these people leave. "We don't have a plan from the government. We don't have anything. We don't even know when they're going to finish screening everyone."The prime minister said on Monday that King Felipe VI would visit Ceuta "as soon as conditions allow", seen as an attempt to assert Spanish authority over the exclave. Morocco has a long-standing claim over Ceuta and its fellow autonomous city of Melilla. The last time a Spanish head of state visited the territories in 2007, Rabat pulled its ambassador from Madrid, and another royal visit may cause further diplomatic tensions.In an interview with Spanish radio channel Cadena Ser, Sánchez made a point of saying the king had not visited Ceuta for 20 years - even though Felipe has only been on the throne for 12 years and it was Juan Carlos who visited in 2007. He also asserted he was the only prime minister to have made an official visit to Ceuta while in office, having travelled there on 31 July as the crisis took hold. Some Spanish commentators noted that his remarks appeared to criticise the king, whom he then met later in the day.Unlike his political opponents, Sánchez has been careful to avoid blaming Morocco for stoking the surge of migrants. He said on Monday that no intelligence reports pointed to "any involvement in one way or another" from the Moroccan authorities.Instead he focused on disinformation on social media "associated with both Russia and Israel and an international far-right movement that always uses migration, not only to attack Spain but also Europe". He told Cadena Ser it did not mean "it must come from a state actor" and appeared to indicate the crisis had been stoked after the influx. Government spokeswoman Elma Saiz later confirmed his allegation, saying there was evidence that "various digital forums amplified what happened with the intention of fracturing and polarising Europe".Russia and Israel have both denied any involvement. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar accused the Spanish prime minister of "a blatant lie" and Russia's foreign ministry spokeswoman demanded proof to support Sánchez's allegations.A large number of social media posts appeared in August portraying the border fence between Morocco and Ceuta as safe and easy, even though at least 100 people died while trying to swim around the border fence, according to figures from the mayor.Spanish fact-checking website Maldita said before 30 July, when the influx began, messages circulated on Moroccan social media encouraging people to attempt the crossing, after a June ruling by Spain's Supreme Court.The opposition People's Party (PP) has criticised Sánchez for "exonerating" Morocco and pointing the finger in other directions. Borja Sémper, a spokesperson for the party, said tens of thousands of people could not have moved towards the Ceuta border without Morocco's knowledge.Morocco has denied orchestrating or being involved in the mass crossing.

schema.headline: Sexual assaults in Ceuta happening almost every day, prosecutors say

title: Newcastle transfer: Matias Fernandez-Pardo joins from Lille for initial £51.4m
description: Newcastle United have signed forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo from Lille for an initial £51.4m.Fernandez-Pardo flew into Tyneside on Monday night to hav
body: Newcastle United have signed forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo from Lille for an initial £51.4m.Fernandez-Pardo flew into Tyneside on Monday night to have a medical and sign a long-term contract.The 21-year-old said he was "very proud to be at such a big club" following talks with head coach Matthias Jaissle."He really showed how much he wanted me to be here," the Belgium international said. "In terms of my own career progression, it made complete sense to come so I didn't hesitate at all.  "I know the club, I know about the stadium, I know it's a fantastic atmosphere. I've followed the team."I'm still young, I'm still hungry, and that's why I'm here, and I want to make that progress with Newcastle. I can't wait to start the wonderful adventure here."Fernandez-Pardo was left out of Lille's squad for the 2-2 draw against Paris St-Germain last week and ordered to train away from the first-team squad until his future was resolved.The forward has been a long-standing target of Newcastle's - dating back to former head coach Eddie Howe's time in charge - and fits the age range the club have been targeting.Of those players aged 21 and under across Europe's big five leagues last season, Fernandez-Pardo ranked second for big chances (21), fifth for touches in the opposition box (184) and shots on target (30), and seventh for goals and assists combined (13).His ability to play in a number of positions across the frontline also made him an attractive target as Jaissle looked to strengthen his squad."Matias is a highly technical player with explosiveness in his game," Jaissle said. "He can score and assist, he has courage, and he has the ability to take players on. "We're sure our supporters will enjoy watching him play. He has already shown in Lille that he can perform on the big stage, and we will work closely with him to keep developing his game further. "We are excited to see him in a Newcastle United shirt."

schema.headline: Newcastle transfer: Matias Fernandez-Pardo joins from Lille for initial £51.4m

title: Alps murders: Luger in a lake gives hope for French cold case
description: Police investigating the unsolved murder of a British family in France 14 years ago have an unexpected new clue with the discovery of a Luger pistol i
body: Police investigating the unsolved murder of a British family in France 14 years ago have an unexpected new clue with the discovery of a Luger pistol in the waters of a nearby lake.One of the few certainties in the killings of Saad al-Hilli with his wife and mother-in-law – as well as a passing cyclist – is that they were shot through the head with a Luger model P06, a type used by the Swiss army until around 1960.Now France's cold case unit has confirmed the discovery of a Luger in Lake Annecy,  not far from the scene of the murders in September 2012.According to Marianne magazine, which broke the story, it was British tourists on 20 August who found the weapon lying in two metres of water.At first they thought it was a water pistol, but realised their mistake when they felt its weight.The discovery was made near the very camping site – Le Solitaire du Lac – where the al-Hillis were staying in their caravan, Marianne reported.Forensic experts are now examining the weapon, which has been badly damaged by its time under water, to see if it is indeed a P06 model.It is estimated that around 60,000 Luger P06s were manufactured. But the number of Luger pistols in general that were made is more like three million.Exhaustive investigations in France and the UK have left police no closer to understanding who carried out the al-Hilli murders and why.  Over the years a series of leads have been pursued then dropped.A British national of Iraqi birth, Saad al-Hilli was holidaying with his family in the picturesque countryside of Lake Annecy in eastern France.On the afternoon of 5 September, his body with those of his wife and mother-in-law were found in their car, its motor still running, on a forest road near the village of Chevaline. A passing cyclist had – like the other victims – been shot through the head.Poignantly, the two al-Hilli daughters, aged four and seven, survived. The older girl had been hit on the head with a pistol butt and was badly hurt. The younger, lying in the car under her mother's skirts, was not discovered till forensic experts began examining the scene many hours later.It was fragments from the pistol butt which enabled police to identify it as a Luger P06. The model is regarded more as a collector's item than a working weapon, which made the theory of a professional hit against the family seem less likely.Lake Annecy is only 50km from Switzerland, where the Luger P06 will have been familiar to older people from their military service. French police said many examples of the gun have been kept by families on either side of the border.Among the theories that have been entertained are that the murders were linked to a family row over money; that they were the work of a motiveless crank; and that the main target was the cyclist.Police were also briefly intrigued by the fact that al-Hilli's wife's first husband – an American – died of a heart attack just hours before the killings in France.

schema.headline: Alps murders: Luger in a lake gives hope for French cold case

title: Enzo Fernandez transfer news: Man City agree fee of £125m for Chelsea midfielder
description: Manchester City have agreed to pay a joint-British transfer record fee of £125m for Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez.Fernandez joined Chelsea from Be
body: Manchester City have agreed to pay a joint-British transfer record fee of £125m for Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez.Fernandez joined Chelsea from Benfica in 2023 for a then-British record fee of £107m, with his latest switch matching the £125m that Liverpool paid for Alexander Isak also on transfer deadline day last summer.The clubs have been negotiating over the past 24 hours and have now reached an agreement.Fernandez, 25, will now undergo a medical ahead of signing a long-term deal at City. Personal terms will not be an issue.Argentina international Fernandez worked with City manager Enzo Maresca during the Italian's reign at Chelsea.Maresca is keen to work with him again after losing a host of midfielders this summer.Fernandez was not involved in Chelsea's 4-3 Premier League win over Brighton on Sunday or their 2-0 Carabao Cup victory against Luton three days earlier, as reports in Argentina suggested he asked to be left out of the squad.Chelsea set a deadline of 17:00 BST on 14 August for clubs to make offers of £120m or more, in an attempt to end uncertainty before the start of the 2026-27 season.It is the second time this summer that City have broken their own transfer record, following the £116m arrival of Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest.Fernandez becomes the fourth player to move to a Premier League club for a fee of at least £100m this summer - following Morgan Rogers (£117m) to Chelsea, Bradley Barcola to Liverpool (£123m) and City's signing of Anderson.

schema.headline: Enzo Fernandez transfer news: Man City agree fee of £125m for Chelsea midfielder

title: Nepal floods: The remote Nepal-China border crossing at the heart of a Himalayan tragedy
description: The video lasts only seconds.A dark wall appears from behind the buildings at Gyirong, on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border. At first, it loo
body: The video lasts only seconds.A dark wall appears from behind the buildings at Gyirong, on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border. At first, it looks almost like a black cloud. Then it gathers shape and speed: water, mud, boulders, ice and rock surging down the valley. The CCTV footage, whose timestamp reads 10:59:53, went viral.For many, it was the first visual evidence of the sheer scale of the destruction that was unfolding.What happened in the minutes that followed is still difficult to reconstruct. But fragments of video and satellite imagery show much of the border complex swept away, with buildings that once crowded the valley floor simply gone.Electronic immigration records from Nepal's Rasuwagadhi border post are filling some gaps, as well as insights from its only surviving staff member. Tika Ram Pokharel, who happened to be in Kathmandu sitting an exam on the day, tells the BBC the crossing was unusually busy when floodwater hit."This is a historic travel route between Kathmandu and Tibet," explains Kathmandu-based hydrologist Ajay Dixit. "The area is geologically vulnerable, characterised by deep gorges and steep rivers that flow at high velocity, carry heavy sediment and can bring down huge boulders."It is a place where pilgrims heading towards Mount Kailash cross paths with traders travelling between Nepal and China, truck drivers, customs officials, tourists and people who live along the border.On the morning of the flood, more than 100 Indians may have been in or around the crossing. At least 275 Indians remain missing in Nepal, according to India's foreign ministry.Nepal's immigration department has been trying to reconstruct who passed through Rasuwagadhi in the final hours before the disaster.Electronic records show that 89 Nepali and foreign nationals had cleared immigration to leave Nepal for Tibet, while four people had registered their entry into Nepal.The immigration system recorded its final transaction at 08:35:03 local time (10:52 Tibet time), less than 10 minutes before the torrent appeared on the CCTV footage at Gyirong.Four immigration employees, including the head of the Rasuwagadhi office, went missing in the floods. His body was later recovered far downstream. The female official who recorded the final transactions is still missing.Among the foreign nationals recorded leaving Nepal that morning were 32 Indians, 12 Chinese nationals and nine Americans, as well as citizens of Britain, Canada, Australia and Italy.Tika Ram Pokharel, the surviving senior immigration assistant at Rasuwagadhi, says the electronic records capture only part of what was happening at the border that morning.The immigration office stood at Ghatte Khola Bazar, about 1.5km north of Timure, a small trading settlement clustered around the crossing. From there, it was another 2km to the Friendship Bridge marking the border with Tibet. Along that stretch were shops, hotels and parking areas where travellers and vehicles gathered before crossing.The Nepalese immigration office opened at 08:00, Pokharel says. Once travellers had cleared immigration, they could continue towards the border or wait in the area before crossing.When Pokharel called a colleague at 08:20 that morning, he was told the crossing was unusually busy. Around 300 to 400 people were waiting to leave Nepal for Tibet, he says, while others arriving from the Chinese side were also in the area."Those who completed the immigration formalities that morning, I don't think were able to complete their immigration process on the Chinese side," Pokharel tells the BBC.Pokharel says it took 15 to 20 minutes to walk from the Nepalese immigration office to the bridge after travellers had cleared immigration. Travellers arriving late the previous afternoon sometimes had to wait until the border reopened the next morning, while those travelling in groups or by bus would often wait for everyone to clear immigration before moving on together.That makes it difficult to know where those 89 people were when the flood struck.At 08:37 - less than two minutes after the immigration system recorded its final transaction - seismic instruments detected movement in the mountains above the border, according to a timeline compiled by Nepal's Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research. Researchers later attributed the signal to the collapse of part of a glacier that triggered the flood.China said the mudslide reached the border crossing from its origin in around seven minutes.People at the crossing could have been making their way towards the bridge, waiting in Ghatte Khola or preparing to cross towards the Chinese facility. Exactly where each person was remains unclear.And Ghatte Khola itself was far more than a waiting area. Pokharel says 50 to 60 houses stood there, alongside hotels, local businesses and four hydropower offices.It was also the final stop for buses from Kathmandu, and a base for drivers, helpers, tourist guides and cargo workers waiting for customs clearance. Travellers heading into Tibet often queued there from the previous day."My 40-50 close friends are missing," Pokharel said. Pokharel believes the toll there could be far higher than official figures suggest, estimating that "2,000 to 2,500 people" may have been caught in the flood. The figure is his estimate and has not been independently verified.The immigration office itself stood about 100 metres above the river, Pokharel says. But during the flood, the water appeared to surge even higher. He initially hoped his missing colleagues might have escaped to grazing land several kilometres away.For some of the Indian pilgrims at the border, the morning had begun almost casually. They made video calls and reels for relatives back home, showing them the mountains as they waited for the Chinese immigration office to open.Sudipto Bhattacharya was receiving messages from his wife, Subhrasree Chakraborty, who was travelling with a group of more than 60 people. At 07:57 Nepal time, she sent him a photograph of the departure stamp in her passport: Nepalese immigration was done. Six minutes later, at 08:03, she sent another message: "We are waiting to enter China." Then the messages stopped.Among those at the Chinese immigration facility was a group of 77 pilgrims associated with the Isha Foundation, returning from Mount Kailash. They, along with three staff members, were unaccounted for after the flood swept through the area.When a 21-member Chinese rescue team reached Gyirong on 28 August, one rescuer told Chinese state media: "As far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins."The crossing had only recently recovered from another major flood. In July 2025, flooding shut Rasuwagadhi for nearly six months. It reopened on 1 January after China built a temporary bridge.Traffic had since returned. Chinese border authorities say more than 100,000 people had passed through Gyirong by June, while Nepali immigration records show 53,742 arrivals and departures at Rasuwagadhi in the year to mid-July. The two figures are based on different reporting periods and counting systems, making a direct comparison difficult.Indians were the largest group recorded at the Nepali immigration point, followed by Nepalis and Chinese.Gyirong had also become one of the main arteries linking Nepal and China.Posh Raj Pandey, chairman emeritus of the Kathmandu-based South Asia Watch on Trade, Economics and Environment, says Rasuwagadhi is one of Nepal's two main trading points with China, alongside Tatopani, and accounts for about a third of Nepal's $2.95bn trade with its northern neighbour.Around 60 to 70 trucks passed through the gorge each day, carrying electronics, machinery, vehicles, fruit, clothing and other goods towards Kathmandu. Pandey says the route also handled about 80% of Nepal's electric-vehicle imports from China.Its closure has left Nepal increasingly dependent on Tatopani - which Chinese authorities have also temporarily closed, external because of landslide risks on the Nepali side, the Kathmandu Post reports. The crossing also lies along the proposed route of the railway connecting the region to Kathmandu, part of plans by Nepal and China to develop a trans-Himalayan rail network."Nepal should develop an alternative China trade route and reconsider its wider development strategy, including its heavy concentration of hydropower projects along the same river system," Pandey says. "We have put all eggs here. We need to develop an alternative border port."Across the border, Pokharel was left thinking about conversations he had with the colleagues who were now missing.The previous year's flood had made staff at the Rasuwagadhi immigration office acutely aware of the danger. At night, he says, they sometimes "felt vibrations" and went outside to check the river. They had even discussed among themselves about escaping uphill if another flood struck."But my friends could not get that chance," he said.

schema.headline: Nepal floods: The remote Nepal-China border crossing at the heart of a Himalayan tragedy

title: I climbed the career ladder and got my dream job at 30 - then I hit burnout
description: Image source, TCOLS StudioImage caption, Jo Hooper said she felt like someone had flipped a switch in her brainByGemma DunstanBBC WalesUpdated 4 hours
body: Image source, TCOLS StudioImage caption, Jo Hooper said she felt like someone had flipped a switch in her brainByGemma DunstanBBC WalesUpdated 4 hours agoJo Hooper spent her 20s trying to climb the career ladder, quickly rising through the ranks with promotions and pay rises."I loved being good at it," said Jo, a former communications professional.But just after she landed her dream role at 30, Jo struggled with burnout and had to take time off work.Burnout, external is recognised by the World Health Organization (WHO) as a state of physical and emotional exhaustion.Recent statistics show 22 million working days, external were lost in Britain because of work-related stress in 2024-25.Jo, now 39 and based in Penarth in the Vale of Glamorgan, said: "I wanted to be a head of communications by the time I was 30, which I did by doing all things you'd expect, working long hours, saying yes to everything including mad things like taking my boss's kids to school."Figure caption, I'm on a mission to convince people to work less"I genuinely thought these were all good opportunities, and I was going to grab them with both hands," said Jo."I remember being in the bathroom crying, hyperventilating, but I never thought 'this isn't sustainable', never thought 'I can't do this any more'."I just thought I needed to change job and I'd be fine. I thought the fix was being in a different organisation but the way I behaved, what I thought was expected of me, was the same everywhere."Jo hit burnout a year into her management role, and it led to two breakdowns within a year."I definitely think it was a case of being forced to stop by my body and mind," she said."I found it really difficult to make decisions, like my brain was working slower. I remember feeling like someone had flipped a switch and my brain had just broken."Image source, Jo HooperImage caption, Jo said during her burnout she could barely sleep and felt sick when brushing her teethImage caption, Dr Jill Williams works with those struggling from burnout after her own experience She said: "It's actually perfectionists or those who go the extra mile who are more likely to experience this."The same traits that get you promoted will be the same ones that burn you out, unfortunately."Public Health Wales' Amy Davies said the phrase burnout could be used interchangeably for stress, but said the two were different things."Stress can feel like drowning, but burnout can feel like having nothing left to swim with," she said.Both experts have helped BBC News bust burnout myths and misconceptions."It's not necessarily just work, we can see it an awful lot in carers and students, any situation where there is long-term stress," said Williams.As it is caused by prolonged, unmanaged stress, it can stem from any persistent, demanding role or responsibility.Is burnout different from depression or anxiety?Burnout and depression are distinct conditions, and the WHO does not consider burnout to be a mental health condition or illness."If burnout experiences are unaddressed it may lead to those conditions developing," said Davies.Will a holiday fix burnout?"Sometimes it can be helpful, but it also needs to come with changes to the context that's causing the distress," said Davies."For many people rest is necessary, but it's not always enough. If you go back to work and your attitude to work is the same, then you're going to have the same result, so something needs to change," added Williams.Is optimisation culture driving us to burnout?Jo Hooper says she's on a mission to convince others to work lessJo ended up leaving her career after she realised it was not sustainable. She was diagnosed with anxiety and depression."I've learnt the hard way that rest doesn't fix burnout, and it certainly didn't fix the breakdown for me. Actually changing the things that burnt you out or broke you down is the only way to get over it."Now I'm a woman on a mission to convince others to work less, because I spent 10 years not doing that, and it nearly broke me."Jo does public speaking and coaching to support business owners and employers to help others avoid reaching burnout."I'm in control, I run my business, I get to decide how it works, I get to decide what I do and who I work with, and that's a huge part of the process for me," she said."I detest this optimisation culture of trying to be as productive as possible. Feeling like we constantly have to optimise ourselves and productivity is just forcing us into working more and living less... I think it just needs to get in the bin."Image caption, Trade union leader Laura Doel said stress is the number one risk at work for union workersSome workforces have raised concerns about staff members leaving jobs due to burnout, including midwifery and teaching.Hannah Leonard, from the Royal College of Midwives union, said: "Midwives do an extraordinary job, and they deserve to feel pride in their profession, not burnt out within a few years of qualifying".Neil Butler from the teaching union NASUWT said: "Changes must be made to bring back the joy into teaching. While it is a relentless grind we will continue to lose good teachers from classrooms in Wales."Laura Doel from Trade Union Congress Cymru, said: "Our research shows that stress is the number one risk at work, higher than traditional dangers like exposure to chemicals, working at height and unsafe machinery."She said actions by employers who offer wellbeing measures are welcomed, but tackling the root cause of stress such as "low pay, insecure contract and impossible workloads" was key.A spokesperson for the Health and Safety Executive, Britain's national regulator for workplace health and safety, said: "Employers have a legal duty to protect workers from risk factors that cause work-related stress by assessing and properly managing key areas of the work."The Welsh government said it was working with employers and trade unions to reduce pressures, support staff wellbeing and ensure appropriate mental health support was available.If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: I climbed the career ladder and got my dream job at 30 - then I hit burnout

title: Jurors in Lindsay Clancy trial deadlocked but  judge asks them to keep trying
description: Jurors in the trial of Lindsay Clancy are deadlocked after three days of deliberations, but a judge has asked them to keep trying.Clancy, a resident o
body: Jurors in the trial of Lindsay Clancy are deadlocked after three days of deliberations, but a judge has asked them to keep trying.Clancy, a resident of Massachusetts, is facing murder charges for killing her three children at their family home in 2023.Her lawyer does not dispute that the 36-year-old former nurse killed the children, but argues that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time and was unable to distinguish right from wrong.The Massachusetts mother is charged with three counts of first-degree murder, as the prosecution argues she made a calculated, intentional decision to kill them. The jury, made up of nine women and three men, began deliberating last week after hearing weeks of testimony from dozens of witnesses. On Tuesday, audible gasps could be heard in the courtroom as Judge William Sullivan read out a note from the jury indicating that it was deadlocked. Clancy, who was left paralysed after jumping from a second-floor window shortly after the killings, appeared stoic as she sat in a wheelchair beside her lawyer.It is not uncommon for jurors in high-profile trials to struggle to reach a decision, and judges have protocols for such situations.A deadlock among the jury such as this one happens in "complex and emotionally charged trials", Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and expert in mental health law, told the BBC."If the deadlock persists, the judge might issue an additional 'dynamite' instruction [known as a Tuey-Rodriguez charge in Massachusetts] to encourage the group to consider alternative perspectives and strive for an agreement while upholding their genuine convictions," Cucolo said.But it is "typically a last-ditch effort" from a judge, she said.The judge can declare a mistrial if the jury is not able to agree on a verdict.Clancy is accused of strangling her kids - Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, who was eight months - with fitness bands in their Massachusetts home  in January 2023. The defence argues that Clancy was experiencing postpartum psychosis, a severe mental health condition that can develop after childbirth, and that she should therefore not be held criminally responsible for the killings.If found guilty of first-degree murder, the intentional and premeditated killing of another person, Clancy will face a mandatory life sentence in prison without the possibility of parole.She could also be found guilty of a lesser charge, including second-degree murder - committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning - or manslaughter - unintentionally killing "by wanton and reckless conduct". In either of those instances, she would face time behind bars.If she is found not guilty by reason of insanity, she will not be set free - she would instead be sent to a psychiatric hospital where her status would be periodically reviewed.  She could stay in hospital for the rest of her life.

schema.headline: Jurors in Lindsay Clancy trial deadlocked but  judge asks them to keep trying

title: As Michigan Senate race heats up, Vance calls Abdul El-Sayed 'evil'
description: US Vice-President JD Vance has waded into Michigan's bitter senate race, calling Democratic newcomer Abdul El-Sayed "evil" as he backs Trump ally Mike
body: US Vice-President JD Vance has waded into Michigan's bitter senate race, calling Democratic newcomer Abdul El-Sayed "evil" as he backs Trump ally Mike Rogers in the closely-fought contest.At an event to support Rogers, Vance also warned El-Sayed to "keep my wife's name the hell out of your mouth", after the candidate appeared to suggest that Vance's late grandfather would not accept Second Lady Usha Vance, who is Hindu. El-Sayed hit back at Vance later on Monday, accusing the Trump administration of pushing "evil" policies and of  "starting wars abroad when there's peace".Recent polling suggests he holds a narrow lead over Rogers in the key battleground state. Speaking at a rally for Rogers in a Detroit suburb on Monday night, Vance repeatedly accused El-Sayed - who is Muslim - of being a divisive figure with little interest in bringing communities together. "I realise that there's something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil and on the rise in the United States of America today," Vance said, adding that he was seeking to "destroy" the country."My message to Abdul El-Sayed is: You can pal around with terrorist sympathisers, and you can say that America deserved 9/11, or you could empathise not with the children who were targeted at Temple Israel, but with the attacker," the vice-president said.During his primary, El-Sayed campaigned alongside controversial far-left influencer and Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who once suggested that the US "deserved" the attacks in New York and Washington. While El-Sayed never said those words and has since distanced himself from Piker, Vance repeatedly linked the two together during his speech. In an interview with CNN later on Monday, El-Sayed took his own jabs at Vance, accusing the vice-president of a series of "evil" policies during the Trump administration. "Evil is ripping healthcare away from working people in exchange for tax breaks for billionaires," El-Sayed said. "Evil is making people pay more for groceries and gas while pushing for trade wars and actual war. Evil is dividing people for your own gain. Evil is selling out your morals for a little bit of power."He also sought to clarify his previous comments about the Vance family and the Second Lady, saying that he was seeking to demonstrate that Vance "believes in a political philosophy that says that some people are somehow more American than others". The Michigan Senate race is among the most high profile of the upcoming midterm elections and takes place in a key battleground state that former President Joe Biden won in 2020 and Donald Trump won in 2024. A survey released earlier this week by Michigan firm Epic-MRA suggests Al-Sayed has a narrow four-point lead over Rogers, a former law enforcement officer with long experience in politics.

schema.headline: As Michigan Senate race heats up, Vance calls Abdul El-Sayed 'evil'

title: Trump says US position on Falklands 'one of many' under review
description: Donald Trump has said the United States' position on the Falkland Islands is "one of many" under review, as he pressed the UK to increase military spe
body: Donald Trump has said the United States' position on the Falkland Islands is "one of many" under review, as he pressed the UK to increase military spending.The US president said the UK has "got some problems, but they'll get solved" when asked about defence funding as a follow-up question to his response on the Falklands.It comes after The Daily Telegraph reported, external US defence officials were drawing up proposals to incentivise Nato allies to meet their spending pledges, with a threat to oppose UK sovereignty over the Falklands among the possible options.The UK government responded by saying Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".A spokesperson added: "The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory and our commitment to them is unwavering."The Falkland Islands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina. The two countries waged a brief but bitter war over the territory in 1982. A British military task force ejected Argentine forces, which had landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim.The 74-day conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.Previous US administrations have formally recognised the UK's de facto administration of the islands, but have not taken a formal position regarding sovereignty.Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump was asked by the BBC if he was reviewing the US position on the Falkland Islands.The president replied: "I always review every position. That's just one of many."Trump's remarks were labelled "nonsense" by Labour MP Dame Emily Thornberry, who chairs the Commons foreign affairs committee, as she asked the UK government to issue an official response in the House of Commons.Foreign Office Minister Uma Kumaran replied: "The UK has no doubt about its sovereignty over the Falkland Islands."They are and will always remain a British overseas territory in line with the wishes of the Falkland islanders."The UK is steadfast in our support for the islanders' rights of self-determination."Kumaran said she had seen Trump's comments, adding: "Our position remains unchanged."The UK government has also faced questions over whether it will continue with a deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and pay to lease back the joint US-UK military base on Diego Garcia.It was confirmed in April that the deal had been paused indefinitely because of Trump pulling his support.Kumaran told MPs on Tuesday that "maintaining long-term operational control and security of the base remains a top priority and is the entire basis for the UK-Mauritius agreement."The minister also said funding for the treaty would be provided for "within the existing spending review settlements" for the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office and the Ministry of Defence.Conservative shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge criticised the remarks and said the deal "belongs on the ash heap of history".He said in a statement: "Burnham should show some backbone and break with this terrible legacy of the Starmer years by ditching his crazy Chagos deal once and for all, and spending the savings on our armed forces."In the Commons, Conservative shadow Foreign Office minister Wendy Morton noted Sir Keir's administration acknowledged in April that the Chagos treaty had become "impossible to agree at political level" and asked what had changed.Kumaran said the Burnham government would "continue to work with the US and Mauritius to find a way forward that is in the UK's best interests and protects our national security".

schema.headline: Trump says US position on Falklands 'one of many' under review

title: Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack
description: Germany has said Russia was responsible for last month's drone attack at Leipzig's airport. A drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Lei
body: Germany has said Russia was responsible for last month's drone attack at Leipzig's airport. A drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany, close to Ukrainian cargo planes, on 4 August.It failed to explode as the detonator was apparently faulty, and investigators suspect a second drone collided with a cargo aircraft nearby. A third drone was reportedly found near the airport 10 days later.Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the Leipzig airport attack followed the "well-established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe" and the assumption was that Germany would be targeted again.He said the that examination of the equipment used along with intelligence findings proved Russian involvement in the attack.German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, who was standing beside Dobrindt at a press conference in Berlin, said he would order the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn, and the contract for the Russian House in Berlin will also be terminated - which many observers have said has been used for espionage and to spread Russian propaganda.He also announced tighter entry controls for Russian nationals and vowed to increase pressure on Moscow's shadow fleet - old tankers used by Russia to circumvent Western sanctions following its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.Wadephul said he had summoned the Russia's ambassador to Germany, Sergei Nechayev. He was seen arriving at the foreign ministry shortly after the announcement.Maria Zakharova, spokesperson for Russia's foreign ministry, said Moscow would respond in a "mirror-image" fashion to Germany's measures."Berlin is sponsoring terrorism", she told the German Press Agency in reference to its military and economic support provided to Ukraine.There have been previous suggestions that the Goethe-Institut in Moscow would have to cease operations if the Germans went through with closing Russian House.Security experts had speculated that Russia may have been responsible, however Russia has always rejected claims of involvement. Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany is used by the Germany military and Nato allies for the transport of military goods and also serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines - which carries most of the country's aerial cargo.The head of Nato, Mark Rutte, said the organisation "stands in full solidarity with Germany"."The evidence is clear. And I welcome the measures announced by Germany in response," he wrote on X.The issue was due to be discussed at a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Ireland later on Tuesday.EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X: "We are united in our resolve to stand against Russian aggression. We will deter anyone who seeks to undermine our freedom and security."She added that the EU was preparing additional sanctions against Russia.Meanwhile, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "Russian attempts to undermine our united resolve and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and doomed to fail."Germany is one of several Nato member states to have reported drone sightings at airports, military and industrial sites over the last year.Berlin has until now been tight-lipped about who may have been behind the Leipzig attack, except to say the "foreign powers" may have been involved. US media had already reported that American officials had linked the incident to Russia.Berlin has warned that the country is the "daily target" of hybrid warfare, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned last week that those who carried out hostile acts against Germany would "pay a price".The government is looking to boost the powers of its intelligence services, which have long been criticised as relatively toothless, to counter such threats.Germany is a key backer of Ukraine with Merz forthright in his support for Kyiv.It is not hard to imagine why Ukrainian cargo planes at a key German logistics hub might be in Moscow's sights.But this announcement comes at a delicate moment for Merz's government.A key state election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt could propel the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) into power at a state-level for the very first time.The AfD, which is Germany's biggest opposition party, wants to stop sending support to Ukraine and re-open ties with Russia.In a separate development, German police say they are investigating the discovery of improvised explosive and incendiary devices at a power substation in the eastern state of Brandenburg on Tuesday.A power line was damaged, which caused a temporary outage. It is not known who planted the devices.

schema.headline: Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack

title: Keir Starmer announces he is standing down as MP
description: Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer has announced he is to stand down as an MP to focus on a role in international affairs.The move will trigger a
body: Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer has announced he is to stand down as an MP to focus on a role in international affairs.The move will trigger a by-election in the London seat of Holborn and St Pancras, long a Labour stronghold, which he has represented since 2015.Sir Keir, who left Downing Street in July, had previously said he would stay on as an MP until the next UK general election, which is not due until 2029.But in a surprise statement hours before his successor Andy Burnham made his debut in the House of Commons, he said he was resigning to work on issues such as international affairs and violence against women and girls.Paying tribute to his predecessor, Burnham highlighted Sir Keir's work with Ukraine and the Hillsborough Law drawn up under his government to improve the accountability of public officials, which is going through Parliament."He has given this country a lifetime of public service, particularly for those fighting for justice," he added. "His leadership took our party from one of its worst defeats to its best victories and created a platform to change this country for the better. We will use it well, and we wish his family the very best for the future."Announcing his resignation, Sir Keir told the Camden New Journal, external it had been a "huge honour and privilege" to represent the London constituency for 11 years, ending weeks of speculation about whether he would remain an MP.He added he was ready to "pass the baton to a successor", telling the newspaper it was the "right time" for him to leave Parliament.He said: "I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world."I will also continue, as I have done for a long time now with others, to work on combating violence against women and girls; that is an issue that matters to me hugely. "It's work I started before I became an MP and it's work I'm keen to continue after I'm an MP. So international affairs on the one hand, and continuing my work on violence against women and girls on the other."Sir Keir became prime minister after winning a landslide majority at the 2024 election, but quit No 10 after pressure from Labour MPs to stand aside.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch wished Sir Keir the best for the future adding: "I can understand why he would not want to spend time with the Labour MPs who treated him so badly after he won them their seats."Tory Party chairman Kevin Hollinrake accused Sir Keir of making "another U-turn having pledged to stay on", prompting a "costly by-election for taxpayers".A date will not be set for the by-election until Sir Keir formally resigns his Commons seat. This will only be confirmed once the government has given him a crown appointment, the mechanism that disqualifies him from being an MP.Labour expects to select a candidate for the by-election by 9 September, according to the party's website.Holborn and St Pancras has long been a Labour stronghold, with Sir Keir securing a more than 11,000-vote majority at the last general election in 2024.Labour's main challenger in the seat is likely to be the Greens, who came second by vote totals at this year's local elections in wards that make up the constituency - with 29.8% of the vote to Labour's 39.5%.Reform UK came a distant third by these vote totals, and the Greens' share was higher if they are given the votes in two wards where they stood aside.Candidates for the by-election will not be confirmed until a later stage, but the Greens hinted that leader Zack Polanski was considering a run at the seat.A spokesperson for the party said Polanksi, currently a member of the London Assembly, had "always made it clear he would like to be a London MP".

schema.headline: Keir Starmer announces he is standing down as MP

title: Breaker Raygun on processing what happened at Paris 2024 Olympics
description: Just hours before representing Australia at the Paris 2024 opening ceremony, Rachael Gunn had a panic attack in the middle of the Olympic village.Thru
body: Just hours before representing Australia at the Paris 2024 opening ceremony, Rachael Gunn had a panic attack in the middle of the Olympic village.Thrust into an environment full of experienced athletes, it dawned on Gunn, whose professional background is as a university lecturer, what she had got herself into.Known as Raygun when competing, she was about to take part in the breakdancing event - or breaking - which was making its Olympic debut."I felt like an imposter," said the 38-year-old breaker, during a new Netflix documentary about her experience at the Games.She describes how she reacted when she saw someone she recognised from the Olympic team."I just could not stop crying... I had a panic attack. 'What am I doing? What have I done? Should I be doing this?'" she said.Just a few hours later, she was sailing down the River Seine alongside the rest of the Australian cohort, waving to onlookers.Less than a fortnight after that, her Olympic journey was over. Gunn failed to win any of her three round-robin battles at the Games, but walked away pleased with how she had acquitted herself."Finishing my last round, the world champion Nicka [Dominika Banevic] gave me props for my moves, the MC celebrated my stuff and the vibe was just generally good," Gunn told BBC Sport.What she hadn't anticipated was that one of her performances, in which she debuted some unconventional moves including a sprinkler and a kangaroo hop, had gone viral.There were memes. There was a sketch on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. Adele referenced the performance in one of her concerts. Chris Hemsworth defended Gunn in an interview with Jimmy Kimmel. At one point in August 2024, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese even felt moved to speak out, praising Gunn for having "a crack"."It was pretty wild the way I became a topic of conversation in spaces I never thought I would be," said Gunn.Alongside the teasing, there were more sinister forces brewing, including conspiracy theories about nepotism - for instance that Gunn's husband and trainer, Samuel Free, had been on the selection committee when she qualified to represent her country at the Games, when he hadn't been."It was really tough when mine and Sammy's credibility, ethics and motivations were being called into question," Gunn said."You could just spend 30 seconds researching and find plenty of sources to debunk these conspiracies, but that's not how people use the internet anymore."That new-found scrutiny took a toll on Gunn's mental health."I felt like my whole life was just kind of crumbling before me.. .and I was just trying to get through the day," she says in the documentary.In the process of making a film about that time, however, she feels that she's been able to regain some agency."It's taken a long time for me to process what happened," Gunn told BBC Sport."It's really exciting for me to finally have a voice again."After it was announced that breaking would be included at Paris 2024, Gunn qualified to represent her country via the Oceania Breaking Championships in Sydney in 2023."I've never participated in anything of such high stakes before. It was all international judges, but I was relieved and excited when I qualified. And then the next whirlwind happened," she said.Quickly, she realised that she would have to start living like an athlete. Gunn gained a scholarship at the New South Wales Institute of Sport in February 2024, which allowed her to begin a strength and conditioning programme."That was great, but also overwhelming because I was training with people who had been doing that stuff since they were kids," she said.In the midst of her training, the documentary reveals that Gunn's mother suffered three brain aneurisms. Gunn herself began a course of anti-depressants to help with feelings of anxiety.The film portrays how it began to dawn on her what she had taken on when she entered competitions in the run up to the Games."That's when it first starting occurring to me that I was going to be going up against world champs and people who had been winning competitions on big stages for years and years, but I was still going to go out there and do my best," she says in the documentary.In that context, Gunn decided to play to her own strengths with a creative gamble, developing a routine that paid cheeky homage to her Australian roots."I was aware that I was never going to beat my competitors on athleticism," she explained."For me, my strength is creativity. With that being one of the [judging] criteria, our thinking was, 'why don't we put all our eggs in that basket and really try and wow them? Maybe we can make a moment.' "We never, ever expected the impact it might have."The documentary reveals that head of the Australian Breaking Association, Lowe Napalan, only assisted Gunn's training "a handful" of times in the build-up to the Games, owing to the amount of administrative work taking up his time.That meant that he only saw Gunn's controversial routine for the first time just before she performed at the Olympics."I was there side-stage," Napalan says in the film."I had to not have a face of shock."It was reported in November 2024 that the furore around her Olympic performance had led Gunn to quit breaking.She corrects that notion."I don't know where that came from," Gunn said."I wouldn't let what happened take dancing away from me. I love breaking, I'll always break, I'll always be a part of the community."Her hope is that the release of the upcoming film can help shift the conversation."It feels nice to lay it all out there and now be able to look to the future. I'm actually excited about what's to come, which is the first time for a while," she said.Details of organisations offering help and support with mental health are available at bbc.co.uk/actionline

schema.headline: Breaker Raygun on processing what happened at Paris 2024 Olympics
